code.title: Route matching: dynamic, catch-all and optional catch-all segments

followUps:
Put the modal in an intercepting route inside a parallel slot, and keep a full page at the real URL. Soft navigation from the feed shows the modal; a refresh or shared link loads the full page.

Layout: app/@modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.js (the modal), app/photo/[id]/page.js (the full page), and app/@modal/default.js returning null. The root layout renders {children} and {modal}. Closing calls router.back().

It makes any param value not returned by generateStaticParams a 404 instead of being rendered on demand. The default is true: unknown values render at request time and are then cached.

Example: you prebuild /blog/a and /blog/b. With dynamicParams = false, /blog/c is a 404. Use it when the set of pages is closed (a fixed list of locales) or when you want to stop crawlers causing endless renders.

Two groups conflict when they resolve to the same URL path, for example (marketing)/about/page.js and (shop)/about/page.js. Both become /about, and the build fails.

Groups never change URLs, so each URL may be owned by only one page. Two groups with different paths are fine. A common surprise is a root page.js in two groups: both mean /. Fix it by renaming or moving one folder.

code.title: Which error boundary catches a layout or page error

followUps:
reset() clears the error state and re-renders the segment, so it works only if the cause was temporary, such as a network blip.

It is not enough when the error comes from a Server Component, because the server data is not refetched by a plain re-render. Wrap it in startTransition(() => { router.refresh(); reset(); }) to refetch and re-render together. If the failure is deterministic (bad data), reset just fails again, so also log it and offer another route.

Because by the time the error is thrown the response status is already sent, so you get a 200 page with a not-found UI and a noindex meta tag instead of a real 404.

Streaming sends headers with the first byte. A notFound() called inside a Suspense boundary happens after that. If you need a true 404 for crawlers, call notFound() before any streaming starts, for example in the page body or in generateMetadata, ahead of the boundary.

Use template.js when you need a fresh instance on every navigation, which a layout does not give you because layouts persist.

Typical cases: enter animations that must replay, per-page analytics in an effect that should fire on each route change, resetting form or scroll state between sibling pages, and a feedback widget that must clear. The cost is a remount of everything below it, so keep it small.

code.title: What can cross the server to client boundary

followUps:
Make the provider its own small Client Component that accepts children, then render it in a Server layout. The children you pass stay Server Components.

// providers.js
'use client';
export function Providers({ children }) {
  return <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>;
}

The layout writes <Providers>{children}</Providers>. Only the provider code is shipped to the browser.

The taint API (experimental_taintObjectReference, experimental_taintUniqueValue) marks a value so React throws if it is passed to a Client Component. It is a safety net against accidentally leaking secrets.

Example: taint the raw user row and the API key, so a careless <Profile user={user} /> fails in development instead of putting the password hash in the payload. It is a backup, not a replacement for DTOs and server-only.

Create a small wrapper file that starts with 'use client' and re-exports the component. That turns the library into a client entry point without editing it.

'use client';
import { Carousel } from 'some-lib';
export default Carousel;

Import the wrapper from your Server Components. Only props that are serializable can be passed. If the library needs callbacks, build a client wrapper component that defines them inside.

code.title: Request memoization vs a tagged data cache

followUps:
Each scenario has a different culprit. Work from the outside in: browser, CDN, route cache, data cache.

  • Navigating back and forth: Router Cache (client). Try router.refresh().
  • Fresh load still old: Full Route Cache, because a static route was built once.
  • Dynamic page old: Data Cache entry not revalidated.
  • Same render shows two values: nothing, since memoization is per request.

Check x-nextjs-cache (HIT, STALE, MISS) to see which layer answered.

You supply a custom cacheHandler (for example backed by Redis) in next.config.js, so every instance reads and writes the same store instead of its own disk or memory.

It must implement get, set and tag invalidation, so revalidateTag on one pod removes the entry for all. Also set the same build id and server-actions key on every instance. Without this, pod A can serve version 2 while pod B still serves version 1 for the whole revalidate period.

A Server Action that calls revalidatePath, revalidateTag or updateTag, or sets cookies, tells Next.js to drop the client Router Cache for the affected routes. The response of the action already carries the fresh RSC payload, so the page updates without a manual refresh.

Example: a form posts, the action calls revalidatePath('/cart'), and the cart UI is replaced in the same round trip. A plain fetch to a route handler does not do this; you need router.refresh().

Log what the server fetches and compare it with a baseline from before the upgrade. Duplicate or repeated CMS calls are visible in logs and in your CMS dashboard.

  • Set logging: { fetches: { fullUrl: true } } and read the cache HIT/MISS lines.
  • Watch requests per minute at the CMS before and after the deploy.
  • Check the build table for routes that turned from static to dynamic.

Then add force-cache or revalidate where you relied on the old default.

Because the old default (cache everything) surprised people: data looked stale and nobody knew why. Making caching opt-in means a page shows fresh data unless you ask otherwise.

It also fit the direction of the framework. Fetches in dynamic routes should reflect the request, and the explicit 'use cache' model makes the caching visible in the code. The trade-off is more origin traffic until you add caching on purpose.

A cacheLife profile is a named set of times that says how long a cached result is fresh and when it may be served stale. Built-in names include seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, max.

Each profile has stale (client may reuse), revalidate (server refreshes in the background) and expire (hard limit). You apply it inside a function with cacheLife('hours') or define your own in next.config.

The page still works for people, but crawlers see only the loading state unless they run your JavaScript, so ranking content should not be client-fetched.

Googlebot can render JS but later and less reliably, and other bots often cannot. If the widget is personal (a greeting, a cart count) this does not matter. If it holds text you want indexed, keep it in the server HTML with Suspense or use cache. Client fetching also adds a request after hydration, which can hurt LCP.

Because Next.js detects dynamic APIs by letting them throw a special internal signal, and a catch block swallows it. The route then wrongly stays static.

try {
  const c = await cookies(); // throws a signal during prerender
} catch (e) {
  // swallowed: Next thinks the page is static
}

Rethrow unknown errors, or keep the dynamic call outside the try.

generateStaticParams chooses which pages are built ahead of time. Pages for other params are rendered on the first request (if dynamicParams is true) and then cached and revalidated like any ISR page.

Example: return the 100 top products. Those are in the CDN at deploy; product 101 is built when first visited and then follows revalidate = 3600. This keeps build time short for large catalogues.

code.title: ISR: stale-while-revalidate with a failing CMS

followUps:
Stage-by-stage: the first request returns the cached page at once, in order to be fast, and the work to refresh it happens behind the scenes.

  • Return only the top pages in generateStaticParams, for example the 50 best sellers.
  • Leave dynamicParams at its default true.
  • Set revalidate for freshness.

The first visitor to a rare page waits for a render (or sees a fallback with Suspense); everyone after gets the cached copy.

Never read cookies, headers or the user session while rendering a page that is cached. A cached page is shared by everyone, so anything personal that was in it is served to the next visitor.

Keep personal content out of the cached shell: render it in a client component that fetches after load, or in a dynamic Suspense hole. Personal data in the URL is also dangerous because searchParams makes the route dynamic anyway. Review any 'use cache' function for request-based inputs.

It makes unknown params return a 404 rather than being rendered on demand and cached. Only the paths from generateStaticParams exist.

With ISR this means the set of pages is fixed after build, but each can still revalidate. Example: you list 3 locales; /fr works, /xx is a 404, and nothing an attacker types can trigger a render.

Put a boundary around each independent block that has its own data, so slow blocks never hold up fast ones. A dashboard might have a header with no boundary, then separate boundaries for the KPI row, the chart and the activity table.

Give each fallback the same size as the final content to avoid layout shift. Do not wrap every small item: too many boundaries cause popping. Place a boundary higher when two parts must appear together.

With Partial Prerendering the first chunk is the static shell, already built at deploy time and served from the CDN, rather than something rendered at request time. It contains the layout and the Suspense fallbacks.

The dynamic holes are filled by streaming in the same response. TTFB therefore looks like a static page (a few ms from the edge), while personalised parts still arrive fresh. Without PPR, the server must render before it can send anything.

A waterfall is when requests run one after another because each waits for the previous result, so total time is the sum. Three 200 ms calls in sequence take 600 ms.

Fix by starting independent fetches together (Promise.all) or by putting each data-fetching component in its own Suspense boundary, so they all start at once and stream as they finish (about 200 ms for all). A real dependency (need user id first) stays sequential; preload what you can.

Next.js uses an Origin check: it compares the Origin header with the Host (or forwarded host), and rejects mismatches. Actions are also POST only, and cookies are SameSite=Lax by default in modern browsers.

If you sit behind a proxy with another domain, list trusted origins in serverActions.allowedOrigins. Action IDs are not meant to be secret, so still check authorization inside each action.

Because actions are queued and sent one at a time per client to keep the results in order. Two quick clicks cannot race each other on the same page state.

The effect is that a slow action delays the next one. So actions are for mutations, not for parallel data loading; use route handlers or Server Components for reads. If you need parallel work, start it inside one action with Promise.all.

Use a route handler when something outside your own React UI must call you, or when you need full control of the HTTP response.

  • Webhooks (Stripe) and third-party callbacks.
  • Mobile apps or other clients calling a public API.
  • File downloads, streaming and custom headers or status codes.
  • GET endpoints that must be cacheable.

For a form in your own app, an action is simpler.

code.title: Middleware matcher patterns

followUps:
Prefer a cheap check in middleware and the full check in your data layer. Middleware sits on every request, so slow work there slows the whole site.

For a static page, make the choice at the edge: rewrite /pricing to /pricing/a or /pricing/b based on a cookie, and prerender both variants. Each stays cached and no render is needed. Use a sticky cookie for a stable bucket, and exclude bots from the test.

Order for an incoming request: headers from next.config, then redirects, then middleware, then beforeFiles rewrites, then the file system (pages, public files), then afterFiles rewrites, then fallback rewrites.

So a config redirect wins over middleware, and middleware can rewrite before routes are matched. When in doubt, test with curl -I and keep rules in one place to avoid loops.

Because middleware runs before every matched request, a database call there adds latency to all pages, and edge code often cannot hold database connections or use native drivers.

Example: a 30 ms query on 1000 requests per second is 30 000 ms of waiting per second, plus a risk of exhausting the connection pool. Check only a cookie or a signed token in middleware, then do the real lookup in the page or API where you can cache it.

Use the Largest Contentful Paint API in the browser, or look at it in tools. web-vitals reports entry.element and entry.url for each real user.

new PerformanceObserver((l) => {
  const e = l.getEntries().at(-1);
  console.log(e.element, e.url);
}).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });

Send this to your analytics and group by page. Lab tools (Lighthouse) show one device only; field data shows what really is the LCP.

Next 16 tightens the defaults: a smaller set of allowed qualities (default 75), minimumCacheTTL raised to 4 hours, local IP optimisation blocked unless allowed, and priority replaced by preload. Check the upgrade guide for the exact list.

The effect is fewer surprise image requests and better cache hits, but images with unusual quality or private-network sources need explicit config.

Bypass it (unoptimized) when the optimiser adds nothing: SVGs, tiny icons, animated GIFs you must keep, or images already resized by your CDN.

Also when you have an image CDN that does resizing better, or when you cannot afford server CPU for transforms. Then use a custom loader that builds the CDN URL with width and quality. Keep the width and height attributes so the layout does not shift.

Anything provided by _app (theme, auth, query client) does not exist in the App Router. You must move it to a client provider component and render it in app/layout.js.

Pages that use useContext keep working only if they become Client Components under that provider. Also getServerSideProps data that used to arrive as props must be fetched in the component. Do both before cutting traffic, or the page renders without its context and crashes.

Each API route file becomes a route handler file: pages/api/users.js turns into app/api/users/route.js. You export functions named after HTTP methods instead of one default handler.

export async function GET(request) {
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}

It uses Web Request and Response rather than req and res, so middleware libraries written for Express-style objects need adapting.

A good honest answer is: the data and state boundaries, not the file moves. Deciding what stays a Client Component and where context lives is where most time goes.

In my experience the pain is third-party libraries without 'use client', tests that assumed getServerSideProps, and caching surprises. Mitigate by migrating one section at a time, keeping both routers running, and measuring bundle size and errors after each step.

Each pod has its own cache, so two users can see different versions of the same page and a revalidation only reaches one pod.

Example: you publish at 10:00 and a webhook calls revalidateTag. It hits pod A only, so pod B serves the old page until its own timer ends. Fix with a shared cacheHandler (Redis) or by putting the revalidate call on every pod. Also prefer a CDN with purge by tag.

Keep the old version's server alive for a while after a deploy (skew protection), and use the same encryption key everywhere so old action IDs still decrypt.

A client with an old page posts an action ID that a new build may not have. Options: route requests to the build they came from (a deployment ID header), keep old containers for some minutes, or return an error that makes the page reload. Never rotate the key at the same time as the deploy.

Pick static export when the site has no per-request logic: a docs site, a marketing page, or a blog whose content changes only on deploy.

You get cheap hosting on any CDN and no server to run. You lose ISR, actions, proxy, dynamic routes without generateStaticParams, and the default image optimiser. If you need one of those, keep the server. Content changes need a rebuild, so link your CMS webhook to the build.
